guided.title: At least one head
guided.prompt: A fair coin is tossed 3 times. List all outcomes with `itertools.product("HT", repeat=3)`, then print the exact probability (as a `Fraction`) of at least one head and the exact probability of exactly two heads on two lines.
guided.starter:
from fractions import Fraction
from itertools import product
outs = list(product("HT", repeat=3))
print(len(outs))
guided.solution:
from fractions import Fraction
from itertools import product
outs = list(product("HT", repeat=3))
print(Fraction(sum(1 for o in outs if "H" in o), len(outs)))
print(Fraction(sum(1 for o in outs if o.count("H") == 2), len(outs)))
hints: Count the outcomes where the event holds and divide by 8.
`"H" in o` for at least one head; `o.count("H") == 2` for exactly two.

guided.title: Conditional from counts
guided.prompt: Counts: 40 customers on plan `pro` of whom 8 churned, and 60 on plan `free` of whom 21 churned. Print P(churn), P(churn | pro) and P(churn | free), each rounded to 3 places, on three lines.
guided.starter:
pro_total, pro_churn = 40, 8
free_total, free_churn = 60, 21
print(pro_total + free_total)
guided.solution:
pro_total, pro_churn = 40, 8
free_total, free_churn = 60, 21
print(round((pro_churn + free_churn) / (pro_total + free_total), 3))
print(round(pro_churn / pro_total, 3))
print(round(free_churn / free_total, 3))
hints: A conditional probability divides by the size of the condition's group.

guided.title: Normal areas
guided.prompt: Scores are normal with mean 100 and standard deviation 15. Print the probability of a score above 130 and the probability of a score between 85 and 115, each rounded to 4 places, on two lines.
guided.solution:
from scipy.stats import norm
print(round(1 - norm.cdf(130, loc=100, scale=15), 4))
print(round(norm.cdf(115, loc=100, scale=15) - norm.cdf(85, loc=100, scale=15), 4))
hints: `norm.cdf` gives the area to the left of a value; pass `loc` and `scale`.
Area above is 1 minus the area to the left.
Area between is the difference of two cdf values.

guided.title: Z-scores of a column
guided.prompt: Compute z-scores of `x` using the sample standard deviation (pandas default) and print them rounded to 2 places with `print(z.round(2).tolist())`. Then print the list of values whose absolute z-score exceeds 1.5.
guided.starter:
import pandas as pd
x = pd.Series([10, 12, 11, 13, 12, 30])
print(x.mean())
guided.solution:
import pandas as pd
x = pd.Series([10, 12, 11, 13, 12, 30])
z = (x - x.mean()) / x.std()
print(z.round(2).tolist())
print(x[z.abs() > 1.5].tolist())
hints: A z-score subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation.
pandas `std()` is the sample standard deviation.

independent.title: Independence check from rows
independent.prompt: `df` has `device` and `bought` (yes or no). Print P(bought), then P(bought | mobile) and P(bought | desktop), each rounded to 3 places, on three lines. Print a fourth line `independent` when both conditional values are within 0.02 of P(bought), otherwise `dependent`.
independent.starter:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"device": ["mobile"] * 50 + ["desktop"] * 30, "bought": ["yes"] * 5 + ["no"] * 45 + ["yes"] * 9 + ["no"] * 21})
print(len(df))
independent.solution:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"device": ["mobile"] * 50 + ["desktop"] * 30, "bought": ["yes"] * 5 + ["no"] * 45 + ["yes"] * 9 + ["no"] * 21})
yes = df["bought"] == "yes"
p = yes.mean()
conds = [yes[df["device"] == d].mean() for d in ("mobile", "desktop")]
print(round(p, 3))
for c in conds:
    print(round(c, 3))
print("independent" if all(abs(c - p) < 0.02 for c in conds) else "dependent")

independent.title: Cut-offs and unusual values
independent.prompt: Delivery time is modelled as normal with mean 48 hours and standard deviation 6. Print the time by which 95% of deliveries are complete (`ppf`, rounded to 2 places), then the probability a delivery takes more than 60 hours (rounded to 4 places). Then for the observed times in the starter print the list of times whose z-score (using mean 48 and sd 6) is below -2 or above 2.
independent.starter:
from scipy.stats import norm
times = [45, 50, 38, 61, 47, 36, 59, 49, 66]
print(len(times))
independent.solution:
from scipy.stats import norm
times = [45, 50, 38, 61, 47, 36, 59, 49, 66]
print(round(norm.ppf(0.95, loc=48, scale=6), 2))
print(round(1 - norm.cdf(60, loc=48, scale=6), 4))
print([t for t in times if abs((t - 48) / 6) > 2])

independent.title: Stretch: simulate and compare
independent.prompt: Simulate 200000 draws of the sum of three fair dice with `rng = np.random.default_rng(7)` and `rng.integers(1, 7, size=(200000, 3))`. Compute exactly, by listing the 216 outcomes, the probability that the sum is at least 15. Print the exact value rounded to 4 places, the estimate rounded to 2 places, and `close` if they differ by less than 0.005, otherwise `far`.
independent.starter:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
dice = rng.integers(1, 7, size=(200000, 3))
print(dice.shape)
independent.solution:
import numpy as np
from itertools import product
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
dice = rng.integers(1, 7, size=(200000, 3))
exact = sum(1 for r in product(range(1, 7), repeat=3) if sum(r) >= 15) / 216
est = (dice.sum(axis=1) >= 15).mean()
print(round(exact, 4))
print(round(float(est), 2))
print("close" if abs(exact - est) < 0.005 else "far")

checks.question: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability of at least one six?
checks.explanation: No six has probability (5/6)(5/6) = 25/36, so at least one is 1 - 25/36 = 11/36. Adding 1/6 + 1/6 = 12/36 counts the outcome (6, 6) twice; the addition rule subtracts it.

checks.question: Of 100 orders, 40 are UK and 10 of those are returned; 20 orders in total are returned. What is P(UK | returned)?
checks.explanation: Among the 20 returned orders, 10 are from the UK, so P(UK | returned) = 0.5. P(returned | UK) = 10/40 = 0.25 is the reverse question, and mixing them is the classic error.

checks.question: For a normal variable, about what share of values lies within 2 standard deviations of the mean?
checks.explanation: The rule is 68% within one, 95% within two and 99.7% within three standard deviations. These apply to normal data, not to any column.

checks.question: Exam A: mean 70, sd 5, a student scored 80. Exam B: mean 60, sd 10, a student scored 78. Who did better relative to their class?
options: The student on exam A (z = 2 versus 1.8)
The student on exam B because 78 is closer to 100
checks.explanation: The z-scores are (80 - 70)/5 = 2 and (78 - 60)/10 = 1.8, so exam A is slightly higher relative to its own class. Raw scores on different scales cannot be compared directly.

checks.question: What does `norm.cdf(1.0) - norm.cdf(-1.0)` return approximately?
checks.explanation: It is the area within one standard deviation of the mean of the standard normal, about 0.6827. 0.34 is one side only, and 0.95 is the area within about two standard deviations.
